text:
Small teams ship faster because they minimize the coordination overhead that slows large organizations. With fewer people, communication is direct and synchronous—decisions don't get lost in approval chains or meeting backlogs. Everyone understands the product vision and owns their piece, eliminating the context-switching required when work passes through multiple handoffs.

Large teams create invisible tax: more meetings to align stakeholders, longer feedback cycles, and diffused accountability. A bug fix might require sign-off from three departments before deployment. Small teams move a bug to production that same day.

Smaller groups also adapt quicker. They pivot on emerging insights without political friction or legacy constraints. Innovation thrives where one person can propose an idea at lunch and implement it by Friday, rather than waiting months for approval.

This isn't about individual capability—it's about information flow. Every additional person multiplies communication paths exponentially. Small teams have fewer paths, less noise, and faster feedback loops that compound velocity.
